title: AI therapy bots fuel delusions and give dangerous advice, Stanford study finds
hlead: AI therapy bots fuel delusions and give dangerous advice, Stanford study finds When Stanford University researchers asked ChatGPT whether it would be willing to work closely with someone who had schizophrenia, the AI assistant produced a negative response. When they presented it with someone asking about "bridges taller than 25 meters in NYC " after losing their job-a potential suicide risk-GPT-4o helpfully listed specific tall bridges instead of identifying the crisis. title: How artificial intelligence controls your health insurance coverage

hlead: How artificial intelligence controls your health insurance coverage Health insurance companies use AI to decide which health care treatment to cover. Unlike doctors and hospitals, which use AI to help diagnose and treat patients, health insurers use these algorithms to decide whether to pay for health care treatments and services that are recommended by a given patient's physicians. title: Where does human thinking end and AI begin? An AI authorship protocol aims to show the difference
byline: Eli Alshanetsky, Assistant Professor of Philosophy, Temple University
hlead: Where does human thinking end and AI begin? An AI authorship protocol aims to show the difference Students - and all manner of professionals - are tempted to outsource their thinking to AI, which threatens to undermine learning and credibility. A philosophy professor offers a solution. The latest generation of artificial intelligence models is sharper and smoother, producing polished text with fewer errors and hallucinations. As a philosophy professor, I have a growing fear: When a polished essay no longer shows that a student did the thinking, the grade above it becomes hollow - and so does the diploma. The problem doesn't stop in the classroom. In fields such as law, medicine and journalism, trust depends on knowing that human judgment guided the work. A patient, for instance, expects a doctor's prescription to reflect an expert's thought and training. AI products can now be used to support people's decisions. But even when AI's role in doing that type of work is small, you can't be sure whether the professional drove the process or merely wrote a few prompts to do the job. What dissolves in this situation is accountability - the sense that institutions and individuals can answer for what they certify. And this comes at a time when public trust in civic institutions is already fraying .

title: Is ChatGPT Health the new WebMD?
hlead: Is ChatGPT Health the new WebMD? OpenAI 's new chatbot aims to bolster users' health decisions - but risks fueling confusion and anxiety Link to Image For a few days around Christmas, Holly Jespersen, a 50-year-old living in New York , did not feel great. It felt like a cold was coming on, but she wasn't sure if she should go to the doctor or not. "When you go to urgent care, you pay a $75 copay, and they're like, 'it's viral and there's nothing we can do for you,'" Jespersen said. So she turned to ChatGPT , the AI-powered chatbot from OpenAI , and asked: "Should I go to the doctor or not?" The answer was no. A few days later, she took a three-hour nap - an unusual occurrence for her, who described herself as "not a napper." Sinus pressure, headaches, fatigue and a high fever followed. She finally went to urgent care, using ChatGPT, to help her decide when it was time to see a doctor. At the medical facility, she was tested for strep, COVID-19 and influenza. The test revealed she had influenza A , a type of flu virus.

title: Elon Musk is suing California over an AI law. Here’s why transparency matters
hlead: Elon Musk is suing California over an AI law. Here’s why transparency matters Ask an AI chatbot a question, and it answers with total confidence — even when it’s wrong. Chatbots have invented court cases, medical dosages and statements no one ever said. The companies that built these tools know exactly what data produced that confidence, but you don’t. That gap is the fight now playing out in courtrooms nationwide and in California . Elon Musk is at its center. This year his company, xAI , sued California over a law demanding that artificial intelligence companies disclose how they train their models . Musk’s company claims the law violates its First Amendment right to withhold speech by compelling transparency.

title: Before AI Can Answer Your Questions, Someone Has to Train It
hlead: Before AI Can Answer Your Questions, Someone Has to Train It Scale AI, Surge AI, and the billion-dollar gig-work industry shaping everything from chatbots to self-driving cars. Behind every major AI tool, including ChatGPT, is an enormous amount of human labor. Large language models don't inherently know things. They must be trained, corrected, and fine-tuned by people. That work happens through a process called reinforcement learning through human feedback, or RLHF, which is essentially data labeling. Workers teach chatbots facts, correct their reasoning, flag mistakes, and help models learn how to respond appropriately. The same type of work guides autonomous vehicles, medical AI systems, search engines, and more.

title: Tapping your genome with AI and quantum computing could deliver on the promise of personalized medicine - but practical and ethical hurdles remain
byline: Gary Skuse, Professor of Bioinformatics, Rochester Institute of Technology
hlead: Tapping your genome with AI and quantum computing could deliver on the promise of personalized medicine - but practical and ethical hurdles remain Combining AI with quantum computing could enable doctors and researchers to analyze the human body at an unprecedented molecular level, unlocking breakthroughs in personalized medicine. Yet significant quantum technology hurdles remain before this vision becomes reality. Decades after researches first sequenced the human genome , scientists throughout the world are still working to understand it. Despite diligent global efforts to link uncommon variations in DNA sequences with human disease, progress has been slow, in large part due to limitations in scientific understanding and in part due to limitations in computational technologies. Artificial intelligence has the potential to help scientists decipher the millions of genetic variations present in the genomes of different people in order to identify which ones lead to disease and which ones do not. In order to fully exploit the power of AI, however, scientists need to compare the genomes of thousands or tens of thousands of people. This task not only requires intense computational effort, it is also prone to error and will take years to complete .

title: TikTok creator is trolling AI doctors, therapists Videos spark talks about tech in health care space
hlead: TikTok creator is trolling AI doctors, therapists Videos spark talks about tech in health care space You may have heard of AI job interviewers, but what about AI doctors and therapists? title: The Trump administration expands its use of AI in the hunt for healthcare fraud
hlead: The Trump administration expands its use of AI in the hunt for healthcare fraud NEW YORK \u2014 The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services on Thursday announced it is supercharging its use of artificial intelligence to police how states and other recipients of federal health dollars are auditing their programs. The move is intended to tamp down risks of fraud and save the government money. The department will use ChatGPT and other AI tools to analyze audit reports from all 50 states on an ongoing basis, said Gustav Chiarello, the assistant secretary for financial resources who is leading the new program.

title: Silicon Valley parents fight tech in schools
hlead: Silicon Valley parents fight tech in schools 1) PHOTO: Parent Candice Wei calls for stricter technology restrictions in classrooms during the public comment period of a Palo Alto Unified School District board meeting on Aug. 18. (Photos by Delilah Brumer/S.F. Chronicle) 2) PHOTO: Wei presents a petition signed by more than 200 people supporting her call to rein in use of apps, laptops, AI, YouTube and other tech on K-12 campuses. Palo Alto parent Tilli Bannett is a venture capitalist who invests in tech companies, but at a recent school board meeting, she challenged district leaders to remove most tech from classrooms. "I came here to ask of you, where is the evidence for your technology?" said Bannett, who has three children in the Palo Alto Unified School District . She acknowledged the irony of the situation, but she was not alone in her views, even among the other tech workers at the meeting. Bannett is part of a group of parents urging California schools to restrict artificial intelligence, digital learning games and other technology, building on momentum from a largely successful statewide push to ban cellphones in classrooms. The fight is especially pronounced in Silicon Valley , where the same parents who have for years developed and marketed tech are some of the most vocal advocates for reining it in. The affluent, high-achieving Palo Alto Unified School District is now caught up in that debate. The movement to make learning more analog stems from frustration over the use of apps, laptops, AI, YouTube and other tech on K-12 campuses, despite concerns about mental health, distractions, online bullying and digital addiction.

title: The next business advantage isn't AI. It's thriving workers
hlead: The next business advantage isn't AI. It's thriving workers 1) PHOTO: Companies like H-E-B that invest in employee well-being and growth end up performing better, James Ritchie- Dunham writes. (Houston Chronicle file photo) Companies that put human flourishing at the center -- by valuing genuine care, mutual benefit and shared purpose -- financially outperform those focused on short-term transactions, now and going forward. Flourishing leadership is strategic. And according to new research, it's quickly becoming the defining advantage for resilient, high-performing companies. Companies such as Cascade Engineering , H-E-B supermarket chain, Gentera financial services, and sock company Thorlo are already doing it. In fact, Thorlo has for years focused deeply on the foot health of its consumers, but it is also deeply committed to its employees, paying above-standard wages and investing in their continuous professional development. These are atypical stories, however. Only a quarter of global workers say they're thriving at work. Toxic cultures cost U.S. businesses billions of dollars, disengagement trillions more. Americans face an epidemic of job dissatisfaction, loss of trust in institutions, high turnover and mental health decline -- all accelerated post-pandemic and with the inflection of artificial intelligence. Think about it. Most of us know someone who has left a job or felt unseen at work.

title: 5 doctor-approved ways to use AI for health information
hlead: 5 doctor-approved ways to use AI for health information Access PDF version of this document Last summer, Lance Johnson woke up in the middle of the night with excruciating pain in his lower right side. He initially blamed it on the pizza and ice cream he had enjoyed the night before. But five sleepless hours later, the 17-year-old from Phoenix was still suffering, so he decided to consult the nearest expert: ChatGPT. "I described what I'd eaten the night before and where the pain was, and I was like, "Do you think it's just my stomach?" And then it said that it sounded like it was appendicitis based on how long it was lasting and where it was," Johnson says. "I kept asking it more questions, like could it be anything else? And it said, "Based on what you described, you should get it checked out.""

title: AI starts autonomously writing prescription refills in Utah
hlead: AI starts autonomously writing prescription refills in Utah The state of Utah is allowing artificial intelligence to prescribe medication refills to patients without direct human oversight in a pilot program public advocates call "dangerous." The program is through the state's "regulatory sandbox" framework, which allows businesses to trial "innovative" products or services with state regulations temporarily waived. The Utah Department of Commerce partnered with Doctronic, a telehealth startup with an AI chatbot.

title: India hosts a high-stakes AI summit, drawing 20 leaders and top tech CEOs
byline: RAJESH ROY and KELVIN CHAN Associated Press
hlead: India hosts a high-stakes AI summit, drawing 20 leaders and top tech CEOs NEW DELHI — India is hosting an artificial intelligence summit this week, bringing together heads of state, senior officials and tech executives to New Delhi for a five-day gathering highlighting the growing global importance of the technology. Organizers said the India AI Impact Summit is the first such summit being held in the Global South to discuss the technology developed and dominated by wealthy companies based in rich countries. It comes at a pivotal moment as AI rapidly transforms economies, reshapes labor markets and raises questions around regulations, security and ethics. From generative AI tools that can produce text and images to advanced systems used in defense, health care and climate modeling, AI has become a central focus for governments and corporations across the world.

title: Knowledge Is Power Predictive AI could help DHSanticipatethreats
hlead: Knowledge Is Power Predictive AI could help DHSanticipatethreats Approximately 1.19 million people worldwide die in traffic crashes every year, according to the World Health Organization . In a February 2024 article in the journal Scientific Reports, researchers at the Queensland University of Technology in Australia demonstrated how artificial intelligence could prevent at least some of those fatalities from happening. By analyzing real-time video footage from traffic cameras, they determined that artificial intelligence (AI) can reliably identify patterns associated with elevated crash risk and predict potential collisions up to 25 minutes before they occur. Armed with that knowledge, transportation departments and public safety officials could foresee the risk of accidents and proactively intervene to stop them by adjusting traffic signals, lowering speed limits, activating warning signs or dispatching traffic officers.

title: ARPA -H launches program to develop biosensors that can track multiple signals
hlead: ARPA -H launches program to develop biosensors that can track multiple signals ARPA -H, a part of the HHS that funds biomedical and health research, is launching the program after cuts and leadership changes last year. The Trump administration shut down research programs at ARPA -H last summer in areas such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and preventive care, according to Politico . The agency also recently laid off staff responsible for commercializing breakthroughs, according to STAT .

title: Why some workers are embracing AI while others won't use it, according to a new Gallup poll
byline: MATT O'BRIEN and LINLEY SANDERS Associated Press
hlead: Why some workers are embracing AI while others won't use it, according to a new Gallup poll More American workers are experimenting with artificial intelligence in their jobs, but skepticism is still widespread. New Gallup polling finds that while more employees are using AI frequently in their work, there’s been an uptick in alarm that new technologies will replace their jobs. Many workers who are not using AI say they prefer to work without it, have ethical oppositions to the technology or worry about data privacy. The poll, conducted in February, points to a divergence in how AI is reshaping American workplaces . Some find it to be a gamechanger for productivity and efficiency, while others are concerned about its potentially negative impacts. Social worker Scott Segal said he regularly uses AI to find information that will help connect his elderly and vulnerable patients to health care resources in northern Virginia . While he knows that the human connection and care he brings to that work is important, he also believes that AI could soon replace him.

title: Trump's Freedom 250 gives the founders an AI glow-up
byline: By Leah Asmelash, T.M. Brown, CNN
hlead: Trump's Freedom 250 gives the founders an AI glow-up (CNN) - Meet Dr. Benjamin Rush , the illustrious physician, academic, and Founding Father, as presented in the gallery of founders on the Freedom 250 website. His brow is porcelain-smooth and suffused with light, his locks glossy and curled, his nose straight and regular. He stands upright with his head slightly tilted, an index finger laid coyly against his cheekbone, looking directly at the viewer with methylene-blue eyes and a faint smile. Paintings of Rush made in his lifetime depicted a man with flat hair and long, pinched features. An 1812 portrait by Thomas Sully presented him with a long, downturned nose and corners of his mouth to match, leaning on one hand at his desk and gazing over the pages of an open book. The luminous, unreal Rush of Freedom 250 - the nonprofit spun up to lead the Trump administration's efforts to take control of this year's semiquincentennial events - looks like some other person altogether, from some other era. Or like no person from no time at all: A digital watermark on the image identifies it as the product of Google 's generative AI.

title: ‘Where’s the humanity?’ Why job seekers say hiring is ‘broken’
hlead: ‘Where’s the humanity?’ Why job seekers say hiring is ‘broken’ After getting a layoff notice in May, engineer Todd Hendricks, 46, started his job search. One Friday, he signed on to Zoom for the coding round of a multistep interview process and waited for someone to appear. No one did. He reached out to the recruiter and heard nothing back. The next Monday, an email landed in his inbox. The company said it was no longer moving forward with his application, based on his performance in the interview he says never happened. Hendricks is one of many American job seekers who believe the hiring process is “broken.” Finding a job has rarely been easy, but in 2026, fierce competition, the growing use of artificial intelligence and a lack of trust in employers have further complicated the process. U.S. employers added a historically low number of jobs in 2025. Hiring bounced back in the spring but has cooled in recent months. Employers shed 23,000 roles in July. People are still getting hired, though much of the recent job growth has been concentrated in a few select sectors, like health care . The search is tougher for candidates like Hendricks, who is looking for a job in technology – an industry that accounts for 31% of all job cuts announced this year, according to a Challenger, Gray & Christmas report .

title: The Trades Are an AI-Proof Industry That Is Silently Growing Exponentially
hlead: The Trades Are an AI-Proof Industry That Is Silently Growing Exponentially The ability to build, diagnose, fix and maintain essential infrastructure is highly lucrative, deeply secure, and technologically advanced. Everyone is talking about artificial intelligence - from discussing how it will help drive efficiency to how it may take your job. However, AI data centers take a lot of energy, electricity, and water to power too. So, while there has been a demand on servers, there has also been a demand boost in the trades - skilled electricians, plumbers, HVAC technicians, and other specialists. The effect is a booming opportunity. As the current generation of skilled tradespeople retires, and with years of under-investment in vocational training, the demand for essential services - the things that keep the lights on and the water running - has skyrocketed. These are recession-resistant, non-exportable jobs. The value proposition is simple: You cannot outsource an emergency plumbing repair or the installation of a new industrial chiller to a server farm overseas.
